segments.text: State responsibility concerns the legal consequences when conduct attributable to a state breaches an international obligation.
The basic framework is attribution + breach, followed by consequences such as cessation and reparation. Circumstances precluding wrongfulness are separate and narrowly framed.
Primary reference: International Law Commission Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (2001).

The International Law Commission's 2001 Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts provide the standard analytical framework. An internationally wrongful act exists when conduct is attributable to a state under international law and that conduct constitutes a breach of an international obligation of the state.

The framework is secondary law: it does not itself define every primary obligation. The underlying duty may come from a treaty, customary law or another international rule. State responsibility asks what happens when that primary rule is breached.

Conduct of state organs is attributable to the state even when a particular official acts unlawfully under domestic law, provided the international rules of attribution are satisfied. Attribution can also extend to entities empowered to exercise governmental authority and, in defined circumstances, to conduct directed or controlled by a state.

Breach is assessed against the content of the obligation in force for the state at the relevant time. The same conduct may breach several obligations, and continuing wrongful acts raise temporal questions about when breach begins and ends.

The responsible state must cease continuing wrongful conduct and may have to offer assurances or guarantees of non-repetition where appropriate. Full reparation aims to address the injury caused and may take the form of restitution, compensation or satisfaction, separately or in combination.

Circumstances precluding wrongfulness—such as valid consent, self-defence, countermeasures, force majeure, distress or necessity under narrowly defined conditions—do not erase the underlying rule. They address whether wrongfulness is precluded in the particular circumstances.

items.text: Is the conduct attributable to the state, and does that conduct breach an international obligation binding on the state at that time?
Attribution connects conduct to the state through organs, entities exercising governmental authority or other recognized legal links. It is different from proving personal criminal guilt.

After breach, consequences may include cessation of the wrongful conduct, assurances where appropriate, and full reparation for injury. Reparation may take the form of restitution, compensation or satisfaction depending on the harm.
Circumstances precluding wrongfulness are exceptional doctrines that may prevent an otherwise wrongful act from being treated as internationally wrongful in narrowly defined situations.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not confuse state responsibility with punishment of an individual offender. It is the international legal responsibility of a state for attributable breaches.

items.text: Do not confuse responsibility with criminal guilt.

segments.text: A state can be responsible for acts of its organs.
Breach is assessed against the international obligation in force.
Reparation aims to address injury caused by the wrongful act.
